idiom_name: node classes with a children method (Prism-style child_nodes)
implementation_notes: Ruby realizes the pattern with one class per node kind and a uniform children method returning the positional child array; generic walking is a visitor passed to accept or a simple recursion over children. Prism, the parser shipped with Ruby 3.4, is the in-tree reference: generated node classes respond to named child methods plus #child_nodes and #compact_child_nodes, and visitors are dispatched through #accept. Data.define (Ruby 3.2+) gives cheap immutable node classes for pure-data nodes. The child method contract replaces the base class, so classic accept/visit is only worth adding when visitors must be pluggable.
code_sketch:
class Node
  def children = []
end

class IntLit < Node
  def initialize(value) = @value = value
end

class Add < Node
  attr_reader :left, :right
  def initialize(left, right) = (@left, @right = left, right)
  def children = [left, right]          # normalized child list
end

def walk(node, &visit)
  visit.call(node)
  node.children.each { |c| walk(c, &visit) }
end
pitfalls: A node that forgets to override children inherits an empty list from the base, so generic passes silently skip its subtree - nothing checks the contract at compile time.
Nodes are mutable by default: any holder can splice children mid-traversal, so freeze nodes (or use Data) when passes assume a stable shape.
Deep recursion in walk, inspect or to_s overflows the stack for large trees; iterative traversal is needed beyond a few thousand nodes.
